    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF THE MIDCONTINENT
                 INDEPENDENT SYSTEM OPERATOR, INC.

        The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) submits1 this Motion for

Leave to Answer and Answer (“Answer”) to the comments and protests filed in the above-

captioned docket by the Midwest TDUs,2 MISO Transmission Owners (“MISO TOs”), the North

American Electric Reliability Corporation and Regional Entities (“NERC et al.”), the Organization

of MISO States, Inc. (“OMS”), Entergy Services, LLC (“Entergy”), Google LLC (“Google”), the

Large Energy Users,3 the Public Interest Organizations (“PIOs”),4 the Joint Consumer Advocates,5

the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”), Rowan Digital Infrastructure, LLC (“Rowan”), and Verrus,

LLC (“Verrus”).

            The comments reflect support for MISO’s Interconnection Reliability Requirements

Proposal (“IRR Proposal”) to establish reliability requirements for Large Loads, while several

parties request modifications or clarification regarding specific aspects of the proposal.6 The

pleadings reflect broad agreement on the central point underlying the IRR Proposal: the

unprecedented scale, concentration, and operating characteristics of emerging Large Loads require

additional visibility and operational reliability tools now. Several parties expressly support the

proposal or its core reliability framework, while other parties seek clarification or additional detail

regarding implementation.7 Notably, only one protest requests the revisions to be rejected and

MISO directed to file revised requirements by the end of 2027.8 And one comment requests that

the revisions be rejected without prejudice to MISO filing a revised proposal.9 MISO believes the

comments reinforce that MISO has put forth a balanced proposal that provides an opportunity to

continue to move forward with the Commission’s desired outcome to support the appropriate

integration of large loads onto the system in a reliable, efficient and transparent way.

           The comments and protests do not demonstrate that MISO’s IRR Proposal is unjust or

unreasonable. Several parties propose modifications to the definitions, transition provisions, or

implementation of the proposed Large Load requirements, while others request that additional

requirements or implementation details be included in the Tariff rather than MISO’s Business

Practices Manuals (“BPMs”).10 These comments present alternative approaches to particular

requirements addressing the necessary visibility into Large Loads and their operation, including

information, modeling, telemetry, and forecasting requirements, while also proposing specific

requirements necessary to address the operational characteristics of Computational Loads.12

         The Commission should therefore accept the IRR Proposal without delaying its

implementation or requiring MISO to expand this proceeding to resolve distinct large-load,

transmission-service, or generator-interconnection issues.13             Accordingly, MISO respectfully

requests that the IRR Proposal be accepted without modification and grant the requested effective

date of December 4, 2026.

I.       BACKGROUND

         The IRR Proposal is an important near-term component of MISO’s broader response to

rapidly accelerating Large Load development. MISO’s 2026 Long-Term Load Forecast shows

load growth at levels not experienced in decades, driven in substantial part by data centers,

advanced manufacturing, and other large-load additions, some of which seek to develop on

timelines materially shorter than traditional generation and transmission infrastructure. 14 The

North American Electric Reliability Corp (“NERC”) likewise has identified emerging

computational loads as an increasing Bulk-Power System reliability consideration because

conventional planning and operational assumptions may not capture the behavior of facilities that

         The Commission’s June 18, 2026 Show Cause Order preliminary found that MISO’s Tariff

appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks sufficiently clear and consistent Tariff

provisions that address certain aspects of the process to provide transmission service to Eligible

Customers on behalf of large loads, including: (1) a definition of large load sufficient to capture

loads that present the unique challenges described in the Show Cause Order; and (2) ongoing

operational requirements for transmission customers serving large loads necessary to ensure

reliable operation of the transmission system.16 In response, MISO proposed Tariff revisions

establishing ongoing operational requirements for transmission customers taking service on behalf

of Large Loads, including hourly forecasts, telemetry and other visibility data, communications,

monitoring equipment, ramp rates, and ride-through requirements.17 The IRR Proposal responds

directly to those concerns through four complementary categories of requirements: (i) visibility

requirements, including data, modeling, telemetry, and forecasting; (ii) PMU requirements for

Computational Loads; (iii) ramp requirements for Computational Loads; and (iv) ride-through

requirements for Computational Loads.18

         MISO recognizes that NERC and industry are working to mitigate the immediate reliability

risks associated with computational load and does not intend the IRR Proposal to unnecessarily

diverge from NERC’s developing framework. At the same time, MISO recognizes that some

          With the IRR Proposal, MISO is proposing to implement one part of a reliability-based

framework to support the interconnection and ongoing operational challenges of Large Loads

within the MISO region. The objective is to establish scalable, technically justified, and risk-

informed expectations that improve visibility into large load behavior, support planning and

operational readiness, and preserve reliable operation of the Transmission System and Bulk

Electric System. The proposed framework is intended to complement existing and developing

MISO planning, interconnection, and operational processes and align, to the extent practical, with

emerging NERC guidance and industry practices.

II.       MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE ANSWER

          Under the Commission’s rules, answers to protests generally are not permitted.26

Nonetheless, the Commission waives this requirement where an otherwise prohibited answer

would clarify the issues under consideration, ensure completeness of the record or assist the

Commission in its decision-making.27

          The comments and protests raise issues concerning the scope of MISO’s Large Load and

Computational Load definitions, the transition framework, the division of requirements between

the Tariff and Business Practices Manuals (“BPMs”), the responsibilities of Transmission

Customers, and the operational forecasting requirements. This Answer clarifies the record on

III.       ANSWER

           A.   MISO’S LARGE LOAD AND COMPUTATIONAL LOAD DEFINITIONS ARE JUST AND
           REASONABLE.

                    1.      The 50 MW Large Load threshold is reasonable, administratively
                    clear, and consistent with emerging industry practice.

           The Commission should accept MISO’s Large Load definition as just and reasonable. As

explained below, the 50 MW threshold — measured at Points of Withdrawal for facilities located

at a single substation— (1) provides an objective, administrable screen for Large Loads; and (2)

reflects specific characteristics of MISO’s transmission system; and (3) ensures necessary

visibility through Section 37A; and (4) does so without a requiring a separate voltage criterion

because applicability is already defined at the Transmission System boundary.

           First, MISO proposes to define a Large Load as Load with Demand of 50 MW or more

associated with a facility or aggregation of facilities located at a single substation behind one or

more Points of Withdrawal from the Transmission System and owned, operated, or controlled by

a single entity or a coordinating group of entities; Load used exclusively for charging an Electric

Storage Resource is excluded.28 MISO determined 50 MW was the appropriate threshold based

on emerging industry practices, the reliability needs of the MISO region, and stakeholder

feedback.29        For example, Southwest Power Pool’s (“SPP”) Commission-accepted HILL

framework uses a 50 MW threshold to evaluate reliability impacts and operational requirements




28
       IRR Proposal at 10-11; proposed Tariff Module A, § 1.L (Definition of “Large Load”); Li Testimony at 11-13.

 for load connected above 69 kV.30 NERC’s ongoing Computational Load initiative likewise has

considered registration thresholds in this range, and the current process is expressly intended to

align new computational-load functional entities with revisions to NERC Rules of Procedure

Appendix 5B.31 Consistent with NERC’s recent developments, a 50 MW threshold is a reasonable

and effective screening criterion, because it is sufficient to identify those loads whose individual

operating characteristics warrants enhanced visibility to determine where specific requirements

may be appropriate to address the identifiable aggregate risks to the transmission system. Further,

a 50 MW threshold is sufficiently material to warrant the Section 37A visibility requirements

because it is consistent with NERC analysis that determined a 50 MW threshold captures the vast

majority of computational load entities that pose aggregate risks to the Bulk Power System.32

         Second, MISO’s footprint includes long transmission lines, constrained flowgates, and a

diverse resource mix, all of which make large, fast-changing loads particularly consequential for

real-time operations. At this scale, a load’s behavior affects not only the local bus but also regional

power flows and stability margins, making continuous visibility essential for reliable operations.

Further, this threshold aligns with emerging NERC Technical Reasoning, which identifies that

large, concentrated, and especially computational loads, exhibit fast-changing, electronics-driven

characteristics that require elevated monitoring and disturbance-performance expectations.33 The

enough that MISO system operators require additional data and performance assurance to maintain

grid reliability. The Commission need not require identical regional definitions, particularly where

the Show Cause Order expressly recognized that an appropriate Large Load definition should

reflect the characteristics of MISO’s transmission system.34 Under section 205, the Commission

evaluates the proposal before it to determine whether it is just and reasonable and not unduly

discriminatory or preferential.35 Multiple approaches may satisfy that standard, and MISO need

not demonstrate that its proposed definition is the only reasonable approach or is superior to

another potentially just and reasonable definition.36

         Third, a 50 MW threshold also is technically appropriate because loads of this size create

material system impacts—such as rapid demand swings, voltage and frequency disturbances, and

dynamic interactions with power-electronic equipment, that cannot be reliably managed without

enhanced modeling, telemetry, and forecasting. Further, the threshold is sufficiently large to

identify concentrated load additions that warrant enhanced visibility and reliability treatment while

providing an objective and administratively clear rule.37 The IRR Proposal also provides clear and

objective      aggregation       criteria—single‑substation           location,      common        or     coordinated

ownership/operation/control, and a 50 MW Demand threshold—which give customers advance

notice of when aggregation applies and allow MISO to administer the rule consistently where

aggregated transmission-system effects.38 Contrary to the Data Center Coalition’s concern that

aggregation is insufficiently objective, the Tariff itself supplies the relevant limiting criteria:

single-substation location, common or coordinated control, and a 50 MW Demand threshold.39

These criteria provide clear notice of aggregation applicability while preserving MISO’s ability to

evaluate the system impacts and coordinated operations of coordinated facilities. These

administrable criteria align with system behavior because the Transmission System is primarily

impacted by the net electrical withdrawal at the point where the facilities connect, not the

individual facilities behind that point. Standard steady-state modeling treats such facilities as an

equivalent aggregated load, and commonly owned or coordinated facilities typically behave as a

unified electrical entity. The single-substation boundary provides a clear, electrically meaningful

point for aggregation while avoiding the inclusion of geographically dispersed and electrically

unrelated facilities. Even where multiple Points of Withdrawal exist, the facilities may affect

shared substation equipment and upstream transmission facilities, resulting in a common or

coordinated system impact. Thus, the Tariff’s objective criteria both preserve notice and reflect

the engineering reality of how aggregated demand interacts with upstream transmission

equipment.

         Fourth, no separate voltage threshold is necessary because Points of Withdrawal bound

applicability across the Transmission System. MISO’s Tariff definition of Transmission System

includes both facilities over which functional control has been transferred to MISO and certain

facilities over which MISO does not have functional control.40 Appendix H of MISO’s ISO

(1) all networked facilities above 100 kV; and (2) All transformers whose two highest voltages

qualify under the above voltage criteria; and (3) all substation equipment that forms the endpoints

Transmission System also includes certain Transmission Owner facilities where functional control

has not been transferred. Therefore, MISO appropriately defines an administrable scope in the

IRR Proposal without duplicative and potentially confusing voltage criteria.

         MISO’s proposed Large Load definition is just and reasonable. The 50 MW threshold is

technically sound, regionally appropriate, operationally necessary, and administratively clear.

Combined with measurement at Points of Withdrawal, it delivers the required visibility without

imposing redundant voltage criteria. The Commission should approve the definition as a

reasonable and well-supported approach to addressing the reliability concerns identified in the

Show Cause Order.

                  2.     The Computational Load definition appropriately targets additional
                  requirements to loads presenting distinct operational characteristics.

         MISO separately defines “Computational Load” as a Large Load comprised of 25 MW or

more of Demand from information technology equipment, such as servers, storage, and networking

hardware.43 This definition serves an important risk-scaling function. All Large Loads are subject

to the transition provisions, to basic facility data, modeling, telemetry, forecast-data, and audit

Computational Loads.44

         That distinction is supported by the record. Computational Loads may exhibit rapid and

coordinated changes in demand, significant power-electronic behavior, and distinct responses to

transmission disturbances.45 The 25 MW computational component provides an objective measure

of material computational content within an otherwise qualifying Large Load. At the minimum

50 MW Large Load threshold, 25 MW represents half of the facility’s Demand, providing

quantitative context for the emerging NERC concept of facilities that primarily contain

information-technology infrastructure.

         The unique and volatile power characteristics associated with Computational Load arise

directly from the function of the underlying facility. Although any individual Computational Load

may, in isolation, appear unlikely to cause a material impact on Transmission System reliability,

NERC has already determined through its Compliance Registry framework that entities which

individually may not pose a material impact on reliability may nonetheless be required to register

for applicable Reliability Standards and Requirements when the class has demonstrated to have

such a such an impact in aggregate.46 MISO’s use of a 25 MW threshold for identifying

Computational Load is directional aligned with NERC’s emerging Computational Load Site

concept, which identifies computational facilities based on the presence of information-technology

infrastructure such as servers, storage, and networking hardware. Within MISO’s 50 MW Large

Load applicability threshold, a 25 MW computational component provides an objective

quantitative indicator that the facility contains material computational content and is therefore

demand changes, software-driven control actions, and power-electronic responses to disturbances.

This objective threshold enables MISO to proactively apply targeted PMU, ramp-rate, and

predictably present, rather than waiting for those behaviors to manifest in operations, which could

expose the system to unmitigated reliability risks.

         Google argues that reliability requirements should turn exclusively on electrical

characteristics rather than end use, and DCC similarly seeks narrower and more predictable

classification criteria.47 MISO agrees with the underlying principle that requirements should

correspond to reliability risk; which is precisely why the IRR Proposal does not impose the

incremental PMU, ramp, and ride-through requirements on every Large Load.48                    The

Computational Load definition is a reasonable proxy for the set of facilities currently known to

present the rapid, coordinated, power-electronic behavior that motivated those requirements, and

the Tariff authorizes MISO to determine whether Computational Load is associated with a Large

Load based on information supplied by the Transmission Customer.49              MISO can refine

implementation as operating experience and NERC standards develop without delaying

protections that the record demonstrates are needed now.50

         B.   THE TRANSITION PROVISIONS REASONABLY PROTECTS EXISTING COMMERCIAL
         ARRANGEMENTS WITHOUT SACRIFICING RELIABILITY.

                  1.    The transition framework directly responds to the Show Cause Order
                  and uses objective Tariff milestones.

            MISO’s transition framework responds to the Show Cause Order by using objective Tariff

milestones to accommodate existing commercial arrangements and agreements nearing

completion. The Commission directed MISO to provide a reasonable implementation period that

minimizes disruption to existing commercial arrangements, allows reasonable time to finalize

ongoing agreements nearing completion when the Tariff provisions are filed, and establishes an

effective date that accommodates those considerations.51 Paragraph 36 of the Show Cause Order

further calls for a reasoned explanation of how the proposal will avoid disrupting existing

commercial arrangements and an identification of a reasonable effective date that accommodates

those arrangements.52        MISO’s framework addresses those objectives through differentiated

treatment based on Service Commencement Date and the MTEP/EPR Condition, rather than

requiring MISO to assess individual private contracts.53

           First, a Large Load with a Service Commencement Date on or before December 4, 2026 is

exempt from Section 37A with respect to the portion of the Large Load that has procured

Transmission Service as of its Service Commencement Date.54            That exemption does not

automatically extend to subsequent increases in Transmission Service. A modification or series of

modifications resulting in a cumulative increase of 25 MW or more, with a Service

Commencement Date after December 4, 2026, may subject the additional Load to Section 37A’s

requirements, depending on whether the additional Load satisfies the applicable MTEP/EPR

Condition and other transition criteria.55 The framework therefore distinguishes the previously

         These milestones are preferable to a project-by-project inquiry into private commercial

commitments. DCC and Rowan propose transition protection based on executed agreements,

equipment orders, investments, or other project-maturity evidence.61 Such an approach is

unworkable for MISO. Treating all agreements as a sufficient determination of project maturity

would render the requirement largely meaningless, as such agreements may not indicate actual

commitment. Likewise, developing prescribed contractual terms and requirements would be

unworkable for Large Loads whose commercial arrangements do not conform to predefined

structures. In the alternative, requiring MISO to make an individualized determination for each

piece of evidence would require a degree of specialized legal knowledge and commercial expertise

that MISO does not possess and could not reasonably acquire without significant staff

augmentation.       Even with additional staff, applying individualized determinations across a

geographical footprint that spans 15 states will almost inevitably involve discretionary judgements

and lead to substantial disputes. Those considerations may be relevant to a developer’s private

economics, but they are not uniform milestones that can reasonably be administered by MISO

under its Tariff. Using private contracts would require MISO to evaluate agreements entered into

and commercial commitments made outside of MISO’s Tariff framework to determine whether

each project is sufficiently mature, introducing variability, disputes, and inconsistent treatment.62

                  2.    The transition provisions are narrowly tailored and preserve MISO’s
                  authority to address material adverse reliability impacts while
                  accommodating existing commercial arrangements.

         MISO’s transition provisions operate within an existing framework of reliability

assessments and local planning and interconnection requirements. MISO’s Transmission Owners

already evaluate load additions through their planning and interconnection processes; ATC, for

example, maintains documented local planning and load-interconnection procedures.64 Section

37A’s ramp and ride-through requirements complement these existing practices by establishing

consistent minimum performance expectations for Computational Loads across the MISO

footprint.

         MISO’s transition framework provides three forms of relief. First, qualifying Large Loads

        MISO's initial ±30 MW/minute ramp limit establishes a reasonable, industry-informed

baseline for managing rapid demand changes from Computational Loads. The limit is intended to

reduce sudden balancing needs and significant changes in transmission flows during stable-state

transitions, while providing a consistent and predictable operating expectation. This initial limit

is informed by comparable industry practices and may be refined as MISO gains additional

operating experience and develops more detailed technical criteria. Because the Transmission

System experiences the aggregate net demand at the applicable Points of Withdrawal (POWs), the

ramp requirement is measured across those interfaces rather than individual computational

equipment or load components. This approach captures the actual impact on the Transmission

System and provides flexibility for eligible associated generation, energy storage, uninterruptible

power supply systems, and other load-management technologies to smooth demand changes,

provided the resulting net ramp complies with applicable requirements.           The ride-through

framework addresses a separate but complementary reliability concern by establishing minimum

voltage and frequency performance expectations during system disturbances. Applying these

requirements with reference to the POWs supports predictable aggregate load response, reduces

the risk of unnecessary simultaneous disconnections, and promotes stable post-disturbance

recovery.

          E.       CONCLUDING ARGUMENTS

          The IRR Proposal should be accepted as filed. It responds directly to the Commission’s

identified operational-reliability concerns, establishes enforceable Tariff obligations for visibility,

PMUs, ramping, and ride-through, scales incremental requirements to Computational Loads, and

provides a reasonable transition framework for existing and in-flight projects.114 The comments

identify implementation questions that MISO is actively addressing through the LLWG and BPM

process, but they do not demonstrate that the filed framework is unjust or unreasonable.

          In addition, the Commission should not delay acceptance of this filing until every related

Large Load issue is resolved. MISO expressly identified that transmission-service products,

enhanced study processes, and cost-shifting protections would be addressed through separate

proposals, and MISO continues to develop those proposals in advance of the Commission’s

November 16, 2026 deadline.115 The immediate operational needs addressed here—that is,

visibility, forecasting, monitoring, ramping, and disturbance performance—exist regardless of the

final design of those later proposals.116
